323.title: Nothing can separate us (Romans 8:31–39)
323.hook: neither death nor life, nor height nor depth
323.howItsDone: Romans 8:31–39 is a reading some families choose for Christian funerals, and some Christians memorize verses 38 and 39 to say in times of fear or loss.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a verse that often gets misquoted, and your line was a good thread in the weave. Not all things are good; they're woven. Did you get to be a good thread for someone? Day three hundred twenty-three.

Losing someone. Being alone. Getting sick. Failing. Being forgotten. Some fears come as a list. Now suppose a friend sits on the edge of the bed and goes through that list, one at a time, out loud. Not brushing anything off. Naming every one. And after each, saying: no, not even that. That's what Paul does at the end of Romans chapter eight. After the groaning and the weaving of the last two days, he lists the worst things he can think of, and lets none of them win. Some people who have never opened Romans know these last lines from a funeral or a wedding.
screen: `SOME FEARS COME AS A LIST.` → `NAMED ONE AT A TIME.` → `NO, NOT EVEN THAT.`

segments.voice: Paul opens with a question, in the King James Bible: "What shall we then say to these things? If God be for us, who can be against us?" Not that nobody will oppose you. Paul had plenty of enemies. But none of them gets the final say. Then he makes a list, and it's not abstract. "Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? shall tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or sword?" In another letter Paul lists his own beatings, hunger, cold and shipwreck, so these aren't abstract to him. And tradition says that Christians in Rome would soon face the sword, and that Paul himself died there. So when he answers, it isn't cheap: "Nay, in all these things we are more than conquerors through him that loved us." In all these things. Not by escaping them. Through them. More than conquerors is one word in Greek, a super-conquering. Then the finale, and it's worth hearing whole: "For I am persuaded, that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come, Nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature, shall be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord." Listen to how he builds it: in pairs. Death and life: the two ends of everything. Things present and things to come: all of time. Height and depth: all of space. And then, just in case he's missed anything, nor any other creature. Everything that exists. None of it can pull us apart from God's love. Then he stops. There is nothing left on the list.
screen: `IF GOD BE FOR US.` · `TRIBULATION, FAMINE, SWORD.` · `MORE THAN CONQUERORS, THROUGH IT.` · `DEATH, LIFE, HEIGHT, DEPTH: NOTHING.` · then, large: `SHALL BE ABLE TO SEPARATE US FROM THE LOVE OF GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read verses thirty-eight and thirty-nine aloud. They'll be on your screen after this. Settle, and breathe. Then read them slowly, out loud if you can, in a whisper if you're not alone. Neither death, nor life. Pause after each pair. When you get to a word that touches one of your own fears, stay there for a breath. Then read the ending once more: shall be able to separate us from the love of God. If you pray, let these words be your prayer. If you don't, let them be something you heard said over you. The bell holds the time.
screen: `FOR I AM PERSUADED, THAT NEITHER DEATH, NOR LIFE, NOR ANGELS, NOR PRINCIPALITIES, NOR POWERS, NOR THINGS PRESENT, NOR THINGS TO COME, NOR HEIGHT, NOR DEPTH, NOR ANY OTHER CREATURE, SHALL BE ABLE TO SEPARATE US FROM THE LOVE OF GOD, WHICH IS IN CHRIST JESUS OUR LORD.`

segments.voice: Super-conquering. The one Greek word behind more than conquerors, Paul's answer to his own list of everything that might separate us from God's love.
Your line: no, not even that. Today, when one of your big fears shows up, name it, and answer it the way Paul does. Day three hundred twenty-three.

324.title: Paul's grief (Romans 9–10)
324.hook: Paul aches for his own Jewish people; how beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news
324.howItsDone: Some churches pray for the Jewish people in their regular intercessions, and the Catholic Good Friday liturgy includes a prayer for them; since the Holocaust, some churches read Romans 9–11 with particular care.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the end of Romans eight: neither death nor life, nor height nor depth. Your line was no, not even that. When a fear showed up, did you answer it? Day three hundred twenty-four.

Someone gets news that changes their life, runs home to share it, and finds their own family sees it differently. Nobody stops loving anybody. It just aches. Paul has just written that nothing can separate us from the love of God. And in the very next sentence, the mood drops like a stone. He's not thinking about Rome anymore. He's thinking about his own family, his own people, the Jewish people. Chapters nine through eleven are Paul wrestling, out loud, with grief and hope at the same time.
screen: `THE BEST NEWS, AND YOUR FAMILY.` → `THE MOOD DROPS LIKE A STONE.` → `GRIEF AND HOPE AT ONCE.`

segments.voice: Paul writes, in the King James Bible: "That I have great heaviness and continual sorrow in my heart." Continual. Not a passing sadness. He says he'd almost give up his own place with Christ if it would help his kinsmen. Then he lists what belongs to his people, and it's a list of honors: "Who are Israelites; to whom pertaineth the adoption, and the glory, and the covenants, and the giving of the law, and the service of God, and the promises." The patriarchs are theirs, and Jesus himself, Paul says, came from them. Paul calls them my brethren, my kinsmen, and he speaks of his people with love. His grief is that his own people, as a people, have not received Jesus as Messiah, and chapters nine and ten turn that over and over, painfully, without easy answers. Then in chapter ten he widens the door: there is no difference, he says, between Jew and Greek; the same Lord is rich to all who call on him. And he asks: how will anyone hear unless someone is sent? And he quotes the prophet Isaiah: "How beautiful are the feet of them that preach the gospel of peace, and bring glad tidings of good things!" Feet. Not faces, not voices. Dusty feet that walked the long road to bring the news. Now something honest. Over the centuries, some Christians used these chapters to look down on Jewish people, and that contempt fed real cruelty. After the Holocaust, the Catholic Church, at the Second Vatican Council, firmly rejected that contempt and said the Jewish people remain dear to God, and a number of Protestant churches have said the same in their own words. Churches still differ on how to understand Paul's hope today. But the chapters themselves open with an ache, not a sneer: great heaviness and continual sorrow.
screen: `GREAT HEAVINESS AND CONTINUAL SORROW.` · `THE ADOPTION, THE COVENANTS, THE PROMISES.` · `NO DIFFERENCE: THE SAME LORD OVER ALL.` · `DUSTY FEET THAT BRING GOOD NEWS.` · then, large: `HOW BEAUTIFUL ARE THE FEET.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for the Jewish people. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind Jewish people you know, or a synagogue near you, or Jewish communities around the world, some of which face real hatred today. Hold them in mind with the love Paul had for his own family. If you pray, you can pray for their peace, their safety and their joy. If you don't, simply wish them well with each breath out. Then think of someone whose feet brought good news to you once, and give thanks for them. The bell holds the time.
Paul's grief. His continual sorrow for his own people, spoken with love, and the beautiful feet of those who carry good news.
Your line: beautiful feet. Today, carry one piece of good news to someone on purpose: a thank-you, a compliment, some news that will lift them. Walk it over if you can. Day three hundred twenty-four.

325.title: The olive tree (Romans 11)
325.hook: Gentiles are grafted into Israel's olive tree; God's gifts are irrevocable
325.howItsDone: Many Christians speak of the Jewish roots of their faith, and some churches mark this with study of the Hebrew Scriptures, Jewish-Christian dialogue, and reflection on Romans 11 during Holocaust remembrance.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Paul's grief for his own people, and your line was beautiful feet. Did you carry a piece of good news to someone on purpose? Day three hundred twenty-five.

Picture an olive tree on a hillside in the Holy Land. Some of them there are centuries old: trunks twisted like rope, still bearing fruit. A farmer who wants a better tree doesn't plant a new one. He cuts a branch, and fits a new one into the wound, and binds it, and waits. That's grafting. The new branch lives on the old root's water and strength. Paul, still wrestling with the question from yesterday, has one more thing to say about his people and the new Gentile believers in Rome. And he says it with a tree.
screen: `AN OLIVE TREE, CENTURIES OLD.` → `A NEW BRANCH FITTED INTO THE WOUND.` → `PAUL SAYS IT WITH A TREE.`

segments.voice: Paul opens chapter eleven with a question, in the King James Bible: "I say then, Hath God cast away his people? God forbid." His answer is no, and he's his own proof: I'm an Israelite too, he says. Then the tree. Israel is a cultivated olive tree, rooted in the promises to Abraham. Some of its natural branches, he says, have been broken off. And Gentile believers, people from the nations, are like shoots from a wild olive, grafted in among the branches, drawing life from the root. Here's the surprising part: that's backward. Farmers usually graft a good branch onto a wild root, not a wild branch onto a good one. Paul seems to know it. He calls it contrary to nature. The Gentiles got in by a move no farmer would make. Then Paul turns to the newcomers in Rome, who may have been getting proud, and he warns them: "Boast not against the branches. But if thou boast, thou bearest not the root, but the root thee." You don't hold up the tree. The tree holds you. And then a line many Christians and Jews in conversation today treasure: "For the gifts and calling of God are without repentance." Without repentance means God doesn't take them back. Paul even hopes the broken branches will be grafted in again, and he says that all Israel shall be saved, though Christians differ on what he meant by that. And then, having thought as hard as he can, Paul stops thinking and starts praising: "O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God!" When his argument reaches its edge, he doesn't pretend to have it all figured out. He bows.
screen: `HATH GOD CAST AWAY HIS PEOPLE?` · `A WILD BRANCH, GRAFTED IN.` · `CONTRARY TO NATURE.` · `THE GIFTS OF GOD ARE NOT TAKEN BACK.` · then, large: `THOU BEAREST NOT THE ROOT, BUT THE ROOT THEE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor your spiritual roots. Settle, and breathe. Think about where your own faith, or your questions, or your sense of right and wrong came from. A grandmother who prayed. A teacher. A congregation. A tradition much older than you, that someone carried to you across centuries. Picture those roots under you, like the old olive tree's. You didn't grow them. They're holding you. Name one of them, and give thanks. If you pray, you can thank God for them by name. The bell holds the time.
Wild olive. Paul's picture of the Gentiles, a branch grafted in against nature, drawing life from Israel's cultivated root.

Your line: you don't support the root. Today, when you feel a little proud of what you know or believe, remember who carried it to you, and thank one of them if you can. Day three hundred twenty-five.

326.title: A living sacrifice (Romans 12:1–2)
326.hook: offer your bodies; be transformed by the renewing of your mind
326.howItsDone: Some Christians begin the day by offering it to God, and some traditions, such as the Catholic Morning Offering, have set prayers for this; Romans 12:1–2 is often memorized.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the olive tree, and the wild olive grafted in against nature. Your line was you don't support the root. Did you thank someone who carried something good to you? Day three hundred twenty-six.

Sacrifice. The word can bring up something dead: an animal on an altar, smoke going up. Or something given up: the sacrifice fly in baseball, the parent who works two jobs. Something lost so something else can happen. Now put two words together that don't seem to belong: a living sacrifice. For eleven chapters, Paul has been talking about what God has done: grace, faith, the Spirit, super-conquering. Now he turns a corner. A small word in his first sentence ties what God has done to how to live. And then he asks for something strange.
screen: `SACRIFICE: SOMETHING DEAD, OR LOST.` → `ELEVEN CHAPTERS OF WHAT GOD HAS DONE.` → `NOW PAUL TURNS A CORNER.`

segments.voice: Here it is, in the King James Bible: "I beseech you therefore, brethren, by the mercies of God, that ye present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God, which is your reasonable service." Start with therefore. Everything Paul asks from here on grows out of the mercies of God he's already described. Not do this so God will love you, but God has loved you, therefore. Then bodies. Not just your soul, not just your Sunday. Your hands, your feet, your tired back, your Tuesday afternoon. And a living sacrifice. Not killed on an altar, but offered and still breathing, going on with ordinary life as a gift. The King James says reasonable service; the Greek can mean the worship that makes sense, or spiritual worship. Translators still argue about it. Then verse two: "And be not conformed to this world: but be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind." Conformed: pressed into a shape, like dough in a mold. Transformed is a different kind of change. The Greek word is metamorphousthe. You can hear metamorphosis in it: a caterpillar becoming a butterfly. And it's the same word the Gospels use for Jesus on the mountain, when he was transfigured and shone. Notice it's in the passive: be transformed. Christians hear that as something God does, not something a person pulls off by effort. And notice where Paul says the change starts: the renewing of your mind, in what a person thinks about and dwells on. In the letter, these two verses open the practical chapters that follow: worship that walks out of church on two feet.
screen: `THEREFORE: BECAUSE OF GOD'S MERCIES.` · `YOUR BODY, YOUR TUESDAY.` · `CONFORMED, OR TRANSFORMED.` · `METAMORPHOSIS: THE TRANSFIGURATION WORD.` · then, large: `BE YE TRANSFORMED BY THE RENEWING OF YOUR MIND.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: offer your day as a gift. Settle, and breathe. Picture the rest of your day, hour by hour. The commute, the meetings, the dishes, the kids, the errands. Nothing special. Then imagine holding it all out in open hands, as a gift. Not a performance. Just this ordinary day, offered. Feel your body: your feet on the floor, your hands. These are part of the offering too. If you pray, you can offer the day to God in your own words, or in silence. The bell holds the time.
Living sacrifice. Not something killed on an altar, but a whole ordinary life, body and all, offered to God as a gift.
Your line: be transformed. Today, notice one thing you let into your mind that squeezes you into a shape you don't want, and swap it for one that renews. Day three hundred twenty-six.

327.title: Love without pretending (Romans 12:9–21)
327.hook: rejoice with those who rejoice, weep with those who weep; overcome evil with good
327.howItsDone: Romans 12:9–21 is sometimes read at weddings and taught as a picture of everyday Christian love; some Christians try to live out "overcome evil with good" by answering wrongs with kindness.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a living sacrifice, a whole ordinary day offered, and your line was be transformed. Did you swap one thing that squeezes you for one that renews? Day three hundred twenty-seven.

A friend texts: I got the job! And somewhere in the chest of the person reading it, just for a second, something can tighten. They wanted that kind of news. They type back: so happy for you!!! with three exclamation points, and they mean it, mostly. Or someone they can't stand has a terrible week, and a small, ugly part of them feels something that isn't quite sympathy. Love is easy to perform. The emojis are right there. Paul, having asked for a living sacrifice, now gets very practical. He fires off a list of short commands, almost like a text thread. And the first one is about pretending.
screen: `I GOT THE JOB!` → `SOMETHING TIGHTENS.` → `LOVE IS EASY TO PERFORM.`

segments.voice: Here's the first line, in the King James Bible: "Let love be without dissimulation." Dissimulation is an old word for pretending. The Greek is anupokritos: without hypocrisy. And a hypokrites, in Greek, was an actor, someone speaking from behind a stage mask. So Paul is saying: let love take off the mask. Then comes the rapid list. Hate what is evil, hold on to what is good. Outdo one another in showing honor. Be patient in trouble. Keep praying. Share with those in need. Welcome strangers. And then two lines that are harder than they sound: "Rejoice with them that do rejoice, and weep with them that weep." Some readers say the weeping is the easier of the two, and that rejoicing with someone whose good news stings is where the mask really comes off. Then Paul goes further, into enemies. Bless those who persecute you. Don't pay back evil for evil. If it be possible, he says, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men. As much as depends on you, because sometimes it doesn't. Leave vengeance to God. And then, quoting Proverbs: "Therefore if thine enemy hunger, feed him; if he thirst, give him drink: for in so doing thou shalt heap coals of fire on his head." Coals of fire sounds like revenge, but some readers hear it as the burning shame of being treated kindly by someone you've wronged, the kind that might change a heart. Nobody's completely sure where the image comes from. And the last line of the chapter sums it all up: "Be not overcome of evil, but overcome evil with good." You can hear Jesus's own teaching behind it: love your enemies, bless those who curse you.
screen: `A HYPOCRITE WAS AN ACTOR IN A MASK.` · `REJOICE WITH THEM THAT DO REJOICE.` · `AS MUCH AS LIETH IN YOU.` · `FEED YOUR ENEMY: COALS OF FIRE.` · then, large: `OVERCOME EVIL WITH GOOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: rejoice with someone today. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone who has good news right now. A promotion, a baby, a trip, a new love, a win. If there's a little tightness when you think of them, notice it honestly; that's all right. Then picture their face when they got the news. Let yourself be glad with them, really glad, not performing. Breathe in their good news like it's partly yours. If you pray, you can thank God for their joy, by name. The bell holds the time.
Anupokritos. Paul's Greek word for love without hypocrisy: no actor's mask, glad with the glad, sad with the sad.

Your line: overcome evil with good. Today, tell the person you thought of how glad you are for them, in your own words, no mask. And if someone wrongs you, answer with one good thing. Day three hundred twenty-seven.

328.title: Owe no one anything (Romans 13:8–14)
328.hook: except to love one another; love is the fulfilling of the law
328.howItsDone: Romans 13:11–14 is a traditional reading for the first Sunday of Advent in some churches, and Christians tell Augustine's conversion story as an example of how a single verse can change a life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, love without pretending, anupokritos, love with the mask off, and your line was overcome evil with good. Did you tell someone how glad you were for them? Day three hundred twenty-eight.

Plenty of friendships run on a quiet ledger. The friend who paid for lunch last time, so it's your turn. The neighbor who watched your dog, so you owe them one. The twenty dollars your brother still hasn't paid back. Score gets kept, often without anyone meaning to, and it feels fair. Paul has just been talking about paying what you owe: taxes to whom taxes are due, honor to whom honor is due. Pay it all, he says, settle up. And then, in the very next breath, he names the one debt you can never pay off. And he says that's the one to keep.
screen: `A LITTLE MENTAL LEDGER.` → `PAY WHAT YOU OWE.` → `THE ONE DEBT YOU CAN'T PAY OFF.`

segments.voice: Here it is, in the King James Bible: "Owe no man any thing, but to love one another: for he that loveth another hath fulfilled the law." Clear every other debt. But love is the debt that stays open. You never get to say: there, I've loved you enough, we're even. An old Christian writer, Origen, put it something like this: the debt of love remains with us always, and we pay it daily and always owe it. Then Paul takes the commandments, don't commit adultery, don't kill, don't steal, don't covet, and says they're all summed up in one line from the law of Moses: love your neighbor as yourself. "Love worketh no ill to his neighbour: therefore love is the fulfilling of the law." Fulfilling in Greek is pleroma, fullness: love fills the law up to the brim. Jesus said much the same when he named the two great commandments. Then Paul looks at the clock. The night is far spent, he says, the day is at hand. Wake up. Cast off the works of darkness, and put on the armor of light. And he ends with a line that has a famous afterlife: "But put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make not provision for the flesh, to fulfil the lusts thereof." Centuries later, a restless teacher named Augustine sat weeping in a garden in Milan. He heard a child's voice nearby, singing, take up and read. He opened Paul's letters, and his eyes fell on these very lines. He wrote later that a light of peace flooded his heart. He tells the story himself, in his Confessions.
screen: `THE ONE DEBT THAT STAYS OPEN.` · `LOVE YOUR NEIGHBOR AS YOURSELF.` · `PLEROMA: FILLED TO THE BRIM.` · `TAKE UP AND READ: AUGUSTINE.` · then, large: `LOVE IS THE FULFILLING OF THE LAW.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pay one debt, even a small one. Settle, and breathe. Scan your life for something you owe. A book you borrowed. Five dollars. A thank-you note. A reply to a message you've been putting off. A call to someone who has always called you first. Pick one, the smallest real one, and decide when today you'll pay it. Then notice the other debt, the one that never closes. Picture someone you love and notice how much you still owe them in love, and owe it gladly. If you pray, you can give thanks for that debt. The bell holds the time.
Pleroma. The Greek word for fullness: love fills the law up to the brim, the one debt that never closes.
Your line: love fulfils the law. Today, pay that one small debt, and then do one loving thing for someone you're not keeping score with. Day three hundred twenty-eight.

screen: `DAY 328 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE WEAK AND THE STRONG.`

329.title: The weak and the strong (Romans 14–15:7)
329.hook: don't quarrel over food and days; welcome one another
329.howItsDone: Christians often turn to Romans 14 when churches disagree over food, holy days, alcohol or worship styles, and some congregations use Romans 15:7 as a motto for hospitality.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the one debt that stays open, pleroma, and your line was love fulfils the law. Did you pay that one small debt? Day three hundred twenty-nine.

Thanksgiving dinner. One cousin is vegan now. An uncle keeps making jokes about it. Someone won't eat before grace; someone else has already started. One sister thinks the holiday should be spent at church, another at the football game. Nobody is doing anything evil. But by dessert, three people aren't speaking. The church in Rome had its own version of this table. Some believers kept careful rules about food and holy days. Others ate anything and treated every day alike. And they were judging each other. Paul, near the end of his letter, sits down at that table.
screen: `A THANKSGIVING TABLE.` → `NOBODY'S DOING ANYTHING EVIL.` → `ROME HAD ITS OWN TABLE.`

segments.voice: Paul starts, in the King James Bible: "Him that is weak in the faith receive ye, but not to doubtful disputations." Welcome them, but not in order to argue with them. He calls one group weak, the ones whose conscience holds them to careful rules about food and days, and the other strong, the ones who feel free. Paul actually counts himself among the strong. But notice where he puts the weight. The strong mustn't look down on the weak. The weak mustn't judge the strong. And whoever's freedom might trip up a brother or sister should be willing to set it aside. "One man esteemeth one day above another: another esteemeth every day alike. Let every man be fully persuaded in his own mind." Each one answers to God, not to the person across the table. Then Paul zooms out: "For the kingdom of God is not meat and drink; but righteousness, and peace, and joy in the Holy Ghost." The dinner matters less than the people at it. And he lands on this: "Wherefore receive ye one another, as Christ also received us to the glory of God." Receive in Greek is proslambanesthe, to take someone to yourself, to welcome them in. The model, Paul says, isn't tolerance through gritted teeth. It's the way Christ received us. Christians still argue about what counts as a food-and-days question and what's more central, and churches draw that line in different places. And some point to this passage when they try to keep a wide table. It's been a week of Romans up close: super-conquering, Paul's grief, the olive tree, a living sacrifice, love without a mask, the debt of love. It all comes down to how we sit at the table together.
screen: `RECEIVE THE WEAK, NOT TO ARGUE.` · `EACH ANSWERS TO GOD.` · `NOT MEAT AND DRINK, BUT PEACE AND JOY.` · `AS CHRIST ALSO RECEIVED US.` · then, large: `RECEIVE YE ONE ANOTHER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: welcome someone who does things differently. Settle, and breathe. Picture someone in your life who practices, eats, votes, worships or celebrates differently from you, in a way that sometimes gets under your skin. See their face. Notice any small judgment that rises, and let it sit, without feeding it. Then imagine pulling out a chair for them at your table, and meaning it. Not to fix them. Just to welcome them. If you pray, you can pray for them by name, and for yourself. The bell holds the time.
Proslambanesthe. Paul's Greek word for receive: to take someone fully to yourself, the way Christ received us at the table.
Your line: welcome one another. Today, when someone does something differently from you, skip the comment, and find one way to make them feel at home. Day three hundred twenty-nine.
